Specific aspects of monitoring are categorized as follows: green indicates that all aspects were observed, orange signifies partial observation or significant shortcomings, and red denotes that the aspects were not observed. Box 5 provides an overview of sector and service monitoring results from an analysis conducted in Serbia. A detailed written analysis of each indicator can help generate more specific recommendations. 2. Factors outside the WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) sector, such as the level of decentralization, are not considered in this analysis, even though they may influence the efficiency and performance of WASH improvements. If the enabling environment analysis reveals insufficient information to fully understand the provision and sustainability of WASH services in healthcare facilities, additional external factors may need to be considered. 3. This approach is adapted from the UNICEF Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene Bottleneck Analysis Tool (WASH BAT). For further explanation, refer to Annex 3. National monitoring data, such as WHO/UNICEF SDG 6 indicators, are used to develop, review, and implement policies and targets at the national level. A national overview of WASH access in healthcare facilities is also available. 4. A policy review should identify all existing standards, policies, and strategies in the health sector that reference WASH in healthcare facilities, whether specific to WASH or related to quality of care. This review may extend to institutional arrangements and partners involved in policy implementation. Both national and subnational documents, as well as existing health systems analyses, should be included. Starting with a key document, such as the national health strategy, and reviewing referenced policies can help identify relevant materials. Discussions with officials may also uncover additional documents. 5. Suggested topics for policy review include health systems, health insurance schemes, healthcare accreditation, private healthcare providers, water and sanitation services, hygiene, infection prevention and control, antimicrobial resistance, maternal and child health, and environmental sustainability. Types of documents to review include regulations, laws, strategic plans, guidelines, and training programs. 6. Understanding barriers to quality of care requires sufficient time for a comprehensive review. Documents may not always be available online, so in-person engagement with staff is crucial. Themes for analyzing policy documents include alignment with WHO or global standards, legal enforceability, accountability mechanisms, and budget considerations. 7. Integrating WASH into national quality priorities is essential. The WHO Handbook for National Quality Policy and Strategy provides a framework with eight national planning elements, which can be adapted to include WASH. These elements guide recommendations to ministries following situational analyses and can also be applied at the facility level. 8. Semi-structured interviews with experts are an effective way to gather in-depth knowledge and experience. These interviews should involve a range of stakeholders, including national and subnational officials, civil society, private organizations, community members, and facility staff. 9. Facility visits are a critical component of situational analysis. These visits validate monitoring data, assess service provision, and evaluate policy implementation. Walk-through assessments provide insights into water availability, sanitation, hygiene, waste management, and environmental cleaning. While not statistically rigorous, they offer a snapshot of conditions and help identify best practices. 10. Data analysis and dissemination should include clear recommendations for action, timelines, responsible parties, and budgets. Stakeholder consultations and national roundtables can validate findings and foster collaboration. 11. Limitations of situational analyses include time constraints, competing priorities, and limited budgets, which may restrict the number of facilities visited. Findings should be verified and triangulated with existing assessments and surveillance data. Facility visits should complement, not replace, comprehensive surveys. 12. Results from previous national situational analyses, such as in Tajikistan, have been used to integrate WASH into national health strategies, action plans, and standards. These efforts have led to commitments from partners and donors to scale up WASH improvements in healthcare facilities.
